title: Are you guys making BIG games with AI?
author: Codingology
selftext:
Do you think AI assistance is enough to produce a game that it would usually take a studio of people to make?  
Or everybody is making fun loop games or short games?

I am currently trying to make a mobile app game. There is not much to do, I just need to polish the models and I should be done, but I wonder if with enough time something great could be made.  
And the answer is “no, you can’t do it with just yourself and AI”, I’d like to team up with a bunch of people that use AI and maybe we could create something big and great together :))

comments.author: Careless_Road8873
comments.body:
Yes, though “big” means something different solo. I’m one person building a medieval turn-based RPG in Godot with AI (Claude for code, image models for art, a video model for the combat animations). Since September it’s grown to a world map with roaming bands, towns, lords and wars, hex battles, companions who bond, grieve and leave, settlements you build up, prisoners, and pets that fight as a pack.

What I’ve learned:

* **AI removes the typing bottleneck, not the design one.** You still decide everything, and you test everything. The hours go into playing, noticing what feels wrong, and describing it precisely.
* **Tests are what make it scale.** My project has 400+ automated tests that run after every change. Without them, every fix quietly breaks something else once the game gets big.
* **Consistent art is the hardest part.** Getting the 50th character to match the first takes reference sheets, strict prompts and fixing things by hand.
* **Scope grows in layers, not in one go.** Ship a small loop, then deepen it. A “studio-sized” game happens through hundreds of small, finished pieces.

So yes, one person with AI can go well past a short loop game, if you treat it as a long project and stay the one who decides. Teaming up can work too, but agree on one vision and one codebase first. That’s where most group projects fall apart.

Good luck with the mobile game. Polish is where it gets good.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
Big games take time to develop, even with AI. It's an iterative process, and AI can't playtest for you. But you're an experienced game developer who knows that, don't you?

(Or what are you doing here?)

Come back in a few months or a year. Or ask the AAA studios what they are building right now. Or maybe, when indie devs who use AI to build games share their experiences on here, read what they write and ask them questions instead of making assumptions and harassing them. That of course assumes you are genuinely interested.

I've been working on a game for half a year in my free time. Without AI, I might have taken at least the same amount of time to get where I am now, but I would have had to quit my real job and work on it full-time. That's not gonna happen. My time horizon is at least another year of development, which may be on and off, because I have a life, too.

If a the games you see are engagement bait, that's a biased view, because of course you see the games that are engagement bait. They are meant to look good and be released fast, not to be playable. You can build playable games with AI, in small increments, at large scale. You cannot one-shoot them, and you will never be able to, because building the code and assets is not even half the job.

comments.author: cratercamper
comments.body:
Mars - partially scientific, partially teleop/AI experiment, partially server-less experiment (secp256k1 curve private keys, bittorent, ghosts as records of all actions, light signing oracles allowing creation of game versions easily via Merkle hashes), partially something else fun (long wild story).   
  
Double full time for 8 months now. Quite works, worst is me adding stuff constantly (recently GPU structural solver and space travel in whole Sol system).   
  
One problem was that Opus didn't know what I am talking about WRT project knowledge - now I have roles like 'graphics' and 'launcher' and 'p\[hysics\]' each role has their own knowledge docs. Also we have com system where the roles communicate with each other (like SendMessage, but with internal archiving) - this also helps with formulating and looking back. Also no trascript deletion after 30 days - Claude can look back months (and it is quite cheap).

Other drag: Claude wanting human to check something ingame that could have been sonnet running the game and checking. But human must know what they want first. Here Linux helps (many game instances running, roles launching these in background for themselves) and also the architecture: whole game is machine-controllable from outside via command server.

And the biggest struggles that took days were with low GPU stuff. Claude routinely says they see something that is in fact not there and you have to be stubborn with what is really there and also with technology you want - if it looks like big work and obscure, Claude will be reluctant to go there. Again, human needs to know what they want. Or e.g. perpective switching with more 2d textures was difficult (zooming out in 2d map blend-switch minimap with the same perspective) or explaining I want 2d map and over it usually invisible 3d data of it but again the perspective must match.

On the good side: Godot works well with Rust and CUDA; Claude knows how to implement a lot technologies by heart (trajectories in space travel, car physics, 3d, physics calculations).

comments.author: uayme
comments.body:
Yes. I'm messing out with AI for 2 months now to see how far i can go, and the results so far are amazing. I constantly increase the scope of what I want to build because AI is just that good.

Right now, a month and a half in into this particular project, a top-down 3d gtalike, I generated over 15k art images and 2k 3d models on my gpu locally, implemented (and refined) a lot of in-game mechanics, added greenery, animations etc.

..but it's still only the beginning. I estimate it's 3-6 months until I have something resembling a game. The hard part is the constant iteration to get a result that is satisfying, and consistent with the rest of the game. Say I have 30 cars in my game right now - each one took at least 10 concept images to manually pick from, and a 2d-to-3d pipeline that took me over a week to refine. And that's not counting over 70 other cars that i rejected on some implementation stage because the end result was not good. 

Each single element of the game demands at least 3 rounds of review and improvements. At least. AI does not get anything right on the first try. That's the real bottleneck.

comments.author: dmarshallgaming
comments.body:
Yes, it's possible to go well past "short loop game" solo, but the AI isn't what gets you there - it's the time.

I've spent about a year on a real-time space strategy game, solo, with an AI coding assistant writing a lot of the code. It has a 10-level campaign, 13 factions, AI rivals that run their own economies, sieges and boarding, an economy with trade and colonisation. That would normally be a small team's game.

What AI gave me: speed. Systems that would take a week took a day, and I could try three versions of an idea instead of one.

What it didn't give me: knowing what's fun, balance, or knowing when something is broken. That came from playtesting - hundreds of hours myself, plus watching other people play and fixing what confused them. The AI will happily build a complicated system nobody enjoys.

So I'd say: the scope ceiling is much higher than it was, but the bottleneck moves from "can I build it" to "do I have the patience to test and cut until it's good". If you team up, team up with people who'll playtest, not just more people prompting.

comments.author: fusionliberty796

It doesn't depend on the AI, it depends on you. A larger vision requires advanced automation pipelines, data management, QA, etc.

For instance, I've been working on my own TCG for a few years now. I now have 6 factions and over 500 cards coded/tested. Well over 10k unit tests, all my own dev tools (card creation, audio, vfx/sfx, cinematics, marketing etc).

replies.author: New-Part-6917
replies.body:
I'm at the point where I feel like all of us working individually on small (but big) projects is a waste of our time in the long run and the real potential will be pooling all of our tokens into creating and refining systems that we can all use in our own projects .. if you know what I mean? I see so many people trying to make a quick buck putting together a tool, system or feature and attempting to sell it and it's fairly obvious AI was used and even which model a lot of the time lmao. That's not to say their product isn't worth money, it's just for many of us intuitive at this point, we build the tools we need now instead of looking for them. Which leads you to think, we are all duplicating these systems over and over again, quietly in our own projects.

 Imagine if even a small percentage of us who have  iterative workflows pooled together and created a serious iterative loop of research, test and refine. Imagine the physics, dialogue, rendering systems we could unlock? It would be slow at first but once it going going and the whole shared system gets refined the outputs would be mindblowing. I believe that is what the AAA studios will be doing right now, laying the groundwork for massively upgraded gameplay systems.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body:
I don't think so based on what I have seen from this sub reddit. The most impressive results are simple to moderate games and prototypes that were prompted quickly. The average is much worse. Many people claim to have spent months vibe coding without much to show for it. The average post here is a simple prototype. No more.

Games that are great and big are incredibly difficult to make. Triple A is often quoted at 100 million. The newest GTA 2 billion.

AI is fast and useful but very limited if you are trying to vibe code in my honest opinion. It is horrible with ideas and creativity. It should fail as the project grows big enough under the sheer size as well as the many errors it made.

I use ChatGPT to make games. But I'm not a vibe coder. I've made several games before AI. I use it through the browser. I maintain a slower speed. I clean up code a lot. Architect. Write stuff myself. Reprompt. And so on. The code just isn't nearly good enough in my opinion. It usually works. But that isn't good enough. It is often much bigger than it needs to be. The interface with which it is used is often bad. It doesn't divide stuff into classes when needed. It doesn't always figure out how best to create helper functions. And many more problems. And this is after all of my planning and detailed instructions.

I suspect the errors and extra size would grow over a larger code base. Individual classes being 30% bigger and worse to use could lead to a project that is 5 times bigger and way more complicated then it needs to be. Vibe coding will simply fail at this point.

And AI just makes too many judgement mistakes. You can't fix this with more prompts or agents or better prompts. The underlying result has issues. Although some results are better than others and it occasionally produces near perfect output. But the average is still a problem. And this isn't a chatgpt vs Claude issue. I've seen some Claude code and it was horrible. And like I said. The code can work perfectly and still be garbage. Individually fine. But as part of a big enough system it will fail.

comments.author: ThaToastiest
comments.body:
Yes, you can - but you will be a human in the loop during the entire process. I've been working on an MMO with a custom engine (started writing the C++ by hand originally) I started in approximately April 2025. I got it to \~50k lines of code before getting LLM assistance - but I was spending context windows sending each thread every single line of code it needed. After 100k lines, I started an agentic workflow and local MCP servers with Claude and Gemini/Antigravity. The game is now live with an alpha (not a lot of content since I am becoming the major blocker, wanting human-made assets at every step of the way) with the basic core loop running live on a Linux server. The MMO features 60hz tick rates, fully deformable voxel terrain, and environmental destruction as combat. The loop: Monster Hunter with a world that remembers your actions.

To summarize: Yes you can, it took me 1.5yrs to construct a pipeline for an MMO that would normally have taken a minimum of 20+ people working across every section of Code (Networking, Physics & Voxel Isosurface Extraction, Synchronization, Serialization, Level of Detail/Area of Interest culling, etc).

https://i.redd.it/w3jzr5ln1nyh1.png

[RiftForged Open Technical Alpha by ThaToastiest](https://thatoastiest.itch.io/riftforged-open-alpha)

comments.author: BranchPy
comments.body:
AI can definitely help you build bigger projects faster, but you still need to review a lot of things yourself. Consistency, missing references, broken flows, forgotten assets, and all the little details are easy to miss when you're generating content at scale.

Full disclosure: I built a QC tool called BranchPy for Ren'Py and Godot projects, and one thing I've learned is that the more content people create (whether with AI or not), the more valuable automated checks become. It catches things like errors, missing pieces, and project issues, but someone still has to decide if the game is actually good.

comments.author: SpecificAntelope5983
comments.body:
I read this thread and I agree with most opinions and personal experiences here, but would like to add one important thing in my opinion. 

I am developer and designer, worked in teams in pre-AI era on medium/AAA games and would never tried to do it on my own before. But now with AI it's possible IF you know exactly what do you want and how to do it before you prompt an agent. And I don't mean "make me a crafting system", I mean that you know exactly what code structure you need, what algorithms, how to do it optimised, have a detailed brief like you would prepare as a game designer etc. Then the AI can follow it exactly and save tons of time, but still you have to code review it so it doesn't collapse under its own weight after few months. And what you can't bypass is testing, balance and mostly UI/graphics which will always be very generic from AI and it will be a cap for a game that aspires to be AAA or somehow big not just in number of players (meaning not something like agar.io etc).

In short if would be able to do it on your own before AI but would take you too much time, now it's possible. Otherwise you will get stuck somewhere along the way.
